claim: Protein feeding is critical for male reproductive success in many insect species.
source: Protein feeding is critical for male reproductive success in many insect species.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of insect reproduction.

claim: Protein ingestion is essential for sex pheromone synthesis in male Bactrocera dorsalis.
source: We show that protein ingestion is essential for sex pheromone synthesis in male.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing sex pheromone detection only in protein-fed males.

claim: Protein feeding or deprivation did not affect Bacillus abundance in the rectum of male B. dorsalis.
source: While protein feeding or deprivation did not affect Bacillus abundance, transcriptome analysis revealed that sarcosine dehydrogenase (Sardh) in protein-fed males regulates the biosynthesis of sex pheromones by increasing glycine and threonine (sex pheromone precursors) contents.
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA gene quantification and amplicon sequencing data showing no significant difference in bacterial abundance.

claim: Sarcosine dehydrogenase (Sardh) in protein-fed males regulates the biosynthesis of sex pheromones by increasing glycine and threonine contents.
source: While protein feeding or deprivation did not affect Bacillus abundance, transcriptome analysis revealed that sarcosine dehydrogenase (Sardh) in protein-fed males regulates the biosynthesis of sex pheromones by increasing glycine and threonine (sex pheromone precursors) contents.
evidence: Supported by transcriptome analysis and amino acid content measurements showing increased glycine and threonine in protein-fed males.

claim: RNAi-mediated loss-of-function of Sardh decreases glycine, threonine, and sex pheromone contents in males.
source: RNAi-mediated loss-of-function of Sardh decreases glycine, threonine, and sex pheromone contents and results in decreased mating ability in males.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments showing decreased amino acid and pheromone levels.

claim: RNAi-mediated loss-of-function of Sardh results in decreased mating ability in males.
source: RNAi-mediated loss-of-function of Sardh decreases glycine, threonine, and sex pheromone contents and results in decreased mating ability in males.
evidence: Supported by mating competition assay data showing reduced mating success in Sardh knockdown males.

claim: Females in many animal species are 'investment breeders', foraging for reproductive resources during adulthood.
source: Females in many animal species are 'investment breeders', foraging for reproductive resources during adulthood, which are directed into offspring production (Stearns, 1989; Stephens et al., 2009; Stephens et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on reproductive strategies.

claim: Males of many species may be categorized as 'investment breeders', depending on foraging success to secure copulations.
source: Intriguingly, males of many species may be categorized in a similar manner (Soulsbury, 2019), depending on foraging success to secure copulations and manipulate female behavior, while prioritizing different resources than the females (Gwynne, 2008; Ng et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on male reproductive strategies.

claim: A number of studies on males from various insect groups suggest a strong link between adult foraging and reproductive success.
source: Indeed, a number of studies on males from various insect groups suggest a strong link between adult foraging and reproductive success (e.g. Lepidoptera [Boggs, 1981]; Orthoptera [Gwynne, 2008]; Mecoptera [Sauer et al., 1998]; Diptera [Yuval et al., 2007]).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies across different insect orders.

claim: The dipteran family Tephritidae contains over 4000 species.
source: The dipteran family Tephritidae contains over 4000 species, and almost all tephritid adults need post-teneral carbohydrate and protein nutrition to realize their fitness potential (Pereira et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a factual statement about taxonomic diversity, supported by established knowledge.

claim: Almost all tephritid adults need post-teneral carbohydrate and protein nutrition to realize their fitness potential.
source: The dipteran family Tephritidae contains over 4000 species, and almost all tephritid adults need post-teneral carbohydrate and protein nutrition to realize their fitness potential (Pereira et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on tephritid nutrition.

claim: The reproductive organs of Bactrocera dorsalis males can significantly enlarge after protein consumption.
source: For example, the reproductive organs (testes, accessory glands, ejaculatory duct, and apodemes) of Bactrocera dorsalis males can significantly enlarge after protein consumption (Reyes-Hernández et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on B. dorsalis reproductive organ development.

claim: In Bactrocera tryoni, protein feeding accelerates the development of the male copulatory apodemes.
source: In Bactrocera tryoni, protein feeding accelerates the development of the male copulatory apodemes (Weldon and Taylor, 2011; Taylor et al., 2013; Reyes-Hernández et al., 2019);
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on B. tryoni reproductive development.

claim: In Ceratitis capitata, protein feeding increases male intensity of sex pheromone release.
source: In Ceratitis capitata, protein feeding increases male intensity of sex pheromone release (Yuval et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on C. capitata pheromone release.

claim: B. tryoni males release an incomplete mixture of sex pheromones when deprived of protein.
source: B. tryoni males release an incomplete mixture of sex pheromones when deprived of protein (Weldon and Taylor, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on B. tryoni pheromone composition.

claim: In many species of Tephritidae, mating competitiveness, mating probability, and mating duration are significantly increased in flies supplied with protein.
source: In many species of Tephritidae, mating competitiveness, mating probability, and mating duration are significantly increased in flies supplied with protein (Yuval et al., 2002; Prabhu et al., 2008; Taylor et al., 2013; Reyes-Hernández et al., 2019);
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on tephritid mating behavior.

claim: Protein supplementation for males increases the amount of sperm stored by mated females.
source: Protein supplementation for males increases the amount of sperm stored by mated females (Taylor et al., 2013; Reyes-Hernández et al., 2019) and the probability of egg fertilization (Blay and Yuval, 1997; Shelly et al., 2002; Yuval et al., 2007);
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on sperm storage.

claim: Protein supplementation for males increases the probability of egg fertilization.
source: Protein supplementation for males increases the amount of sperm stored by mated females (Taylor et al., 2013; Reyes-Hernández et al., 2019) and the probability of egg fertilization (Blay and Yuval, 1997; Shelly et al., 2002; Yuval et al., 2007);
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on egg fertilization.

claim: Ejaculates of protein-fed males inhibit the remating behavior of females.
source: Ejaculates of protein-fed males inhibit the remating behavior of females (Radhakrishnan and Taylor, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on female remating behavior.

claim: The remating rate in females increases significantly when males lack access to protein.
source: Conversely, the remating rate in females increases significantly when males lack access to protein (Yuval et al., 2002; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on female remating rates.

claim: Males of the oriental fruit fly, B. dorsalis, attract females by emitting a pheromone produced by bacteria in the rectal glands.
source: Males of the oriental fruit fly, B. dorsalis, one of the most economically important tephritid species, attract females by emitting a pheromone produced by bacteria in the rectal glands (Ren et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on B. dorsalis pheromone production.

claim: The pheromone of B. dorsalis has been identified as a cocktail of trimethylpyrazine (TMP) and tetramethylpyrazine (TTMP).
source: The pheromone has been identified as a cocktail of trimethylpyrazine (TMP) and tetramethylpyrazine (TTMP), and the pathway of sex pheromone biosynthesis has been proposed in a previous study (Zhang et al., 2019, Ren et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on pheromone identification.

claim: The pathway of sex pheromone biosynthesis in B. dorsalis has been proposed in a previous study.
source: The pheromone has been identified as a cocktail of trimethylpyrazine (TMP) and tetramethylpyrazine (TTMP), and the pathway of sex pheromone biosynthesis has been proposed in a previous study (Zhang et al., 2019, Ren et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on pheromone biosynthesis pathways.

claim: Sex pheromone-producing Bacillus in B. dorsalis have been identified.
source: Although sex pheromone-producing Bacillus in B. dorsalis have been identified, the source of the precursors has not been determined.
evidence: Supported by reference to previous research identifying the bacteria.

claim: The source of the precursors for sex pheromone biosynthesis in B. dorsalis has not been determined prior to this study.
source: Although sex pheromone-producing Bacillus in B. dorsalis have been identified, the source of the precursors has not been determined.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Protein feeding has a significant influence on the reproductive performance of B. dorsalis males.
source: Given that protein feeding has a significant influence on the reproductive performance of B. dorsalis males (Shelly and Edu, 2007), we hypothesized that protein feeding in B. dorsalis mediates sex pheromone biosynthesis by affecting the precursor substance content in the rectum.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on B. dorsalis reproductive performance.

claim: Protein feeding in B. dorsalis mediates sex pheromone biosynthesis by affecting the precursor substance content in the rectum.
source: Given that protein feeding has a significant influence on the reproductive performance of B. dorsalis males (Shelly and Edu, 2007), we hypothesized that protein feeding in B. dorsalis mediates sex pheromone biosynthesis by affecting the precursor substance content in the rectum.
evidence: This is the hypothesis of the study, which is then tested experimentally.

claim: Protein feeding is the key factor that controls sex pheromone biosynthesis in the male rectum of B. dorsalis.
source: The results indicate that protein feeding is the key factor that controls sex pheromone biosynthesis in the male rectum.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing sex pheromone production only in protein-fed males.

claim: Ingested protein supplies the glycine and threonine pathway and provides substrates for sex pheromone production.
source: Ingested protein supplies the glycine and threonine pathway and provides substrates for sex pheromone production.
evidence: Supported by amino acid content measurements and transcriptome analysis showing increased glycine and threonine in protein-fed males.

claim: Different types of sugars had no effect on survival of mature male B. dorsalis.
source: The results showed that different types of sugars had no effect on survival, rectum width, sex pheromone biosynthesis, and mating ability of mature male (12 d old; Figure 1B–G).
evidence: Supported by survival data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Different types of sugars had no effect on rectum width of mature male B. dorsalis.
source: The results showed that different types of sugars had no effect on survival, rectum width, sex pheromone biosynthesis, and mating ability of mature male (12 d old; Figure 1B–G).
evidence: Supported by rectum width measurements presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Different types of sugars had no effect on sex pheromone biosynthesis of mature male B. dorsalis.
source: The results showed that different types of sugars had no effect on survival, rectum width, sex pheromone biosynthesis, and mating ability of mature male (12 d old; Figure 1B–G).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data presented in Figure 1D showing similar pheromone production across sugar types when protein is provided.

claim: Different types of sugars had no effect on mating ability of mature male B. dorsalis.
source: The results showed that different types of sugars had no effect on survival, rectum width, sex pheromone biosynthesis, and mating ability of mature male (12 d old; Figure 1B–G).
evidence: Supported by mating ability data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: Protein feeding did not affect the survival of male B. dorsalis.
source: Though protein feeding also did not affect the survival and rectum width of the males (Figure 1B and C), major products with the same retention time were only detected in YH-supplemented male rectums when rectal extracts were analyzed by gas chromatography‒mass spectrometry (GC‒MS; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by survival data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Protein feeding did not affect the rectum width of male B. dorsalis.
source: Though protein feeding also did not affect the survival and rectum width of the males (Figure 1B and C), major products with the same retention time were only detected in YH-supplemented male rectums when rectal extracts were analyzed by gas chromatography‒mass spectrometry (GC‒MS; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by rectum width measurements presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Major products with the same retention time were only detected in YH-supplemented male rectums.
source: Though protein feeding also did not affect the survival and rectum width of the males (Figure 1B and C), major products with the same retention time were only detected in YH-supplemented male rectums when rectal extracts were analyzed by gas chromatography‒mass spectrometry (GC‒MS; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS chromatograms presented in Figure 1D.

claim: The products detected in YH-supplemented male rectums were tentatively identified as TMP and TTMP based on their mass spectra.
source: These products were tentatively identified as TMP and TTMP in all three YH-supplemented cases based on their mass spectra (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by mass spectra data presented in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The mating ability of males deprived of YH was significantly lower than that of males fed with YH.
source: And the mating ability of the males deprived of YH was significantly lower than that of the males fed with YH (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by mating competition assay data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: Protein feeding instead of sugar type can significantly affect the male reproductive performance (sex pheromone synthesis and mating ability).
source: These results indicate that protein feeding instead of sugar type can significantly affect the male reproductive performance (sex pheromone synthesis and mating ability).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing effects of protein but not sugar type.

claim: Sex pheromones are synthesized by rectal Bacillus using glucose and amino acids as precursors.
source: Given that sex pheromones are synthesized by rectal Bacillus using glucose and amino acids as precursors (Ren et al., 2021), we infer that dietary proteins may influence sex pheromone synthesis and mating ability by influencing the abundance of Bacillus in the rectum or the amount of the precursors.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on pheromone biosynthesis.

claim: Dietary proteins may influence sex pheromone synthesis and mating ability by influencing the abundance of Bacillus in the rectum or the amount of the precursors.
source: Given that sex pheromones are synthesized by rectal Bacillus using glucose and amino acids as precursors (Ren et al., 2021), we infer that dietary proteins may influence sex pheromone synthesis and mating ability by influencing the abundance of Bacillus in the rectum or the amount of the precursors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from previous knowledge about pheromone biosynthesis.

claim: There is no significant difference for total bacteria contents between YH-supplemented and YH-deprived male rectum.
source: The results showed that there is no significant difference for total bacteria contents between YH-supplemented and YH-deprived male rectum (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA gene qPCR data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Microbial communities at the class level in YH-supplemented male rectum were similar with those in YH-deprived male rectum.
source: 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing results showed that microbial communities at the class level in YH-supplemented male rectum were similar with those in YH-deprived male rectum, especially the abundance of Bacilli was very similar (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing data presented in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The abundance of Bacilli was very similar between YH-supplemented and YH-deprived male rectum.
source: 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing results showed that microbial communities at the class level in YH-supplemented male rectum were similar with those in YH-deprived male rectum, especially the abundance of Bacilli was very similar (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Protein feeding had no influence on microbial diversity except in males feeding on sucrose.
source: Alpha diversity in 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing also indicated that protein feeding had no influence on diversity except the males feeding on sucrose (Supplementary file 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by alpha diversity analysis presented in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Protein intake may not affect the abundance of Bacillus synthesizing pheromones in the rectum.
source: These results indicate that protein intake may not affect the abundance of Bacillus synthesizing pheromones in the rectum, and sex pheromone loss in YH-deprived males may not be associated with Bacillus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bacterial abundance and diversity data.

claim: Sex pheromone loss in YH-deprived males may not be associated with Bacillus.
source: These results indicate that protein intake may not affect the abundance of Bacillus synthesizing pheromones in the rectum, and sex pheromone loss in YH-deprived males may not be associated with Bacillus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bacterial abundance data showing no difference between protein-fed and protein-deprived males.

claim: YH feeding only increased glucose contents in males in the sucrose and fructose groups.
source: The results showed that YH feeding only increased glucose contents in males in the sucrose and fructose groups (Figure 2D), which indicates that increased rectal glucose content caused by protein supplementation may not be the main factor affecting sex pheromones synthesis.
evidence: Supported by glucose content measurements presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Increased rectal glucose content caused by protein supplementation may not be the main factor affecting sex pheromones synthesis.
source: The results showed that YH feeding only increased glucose contents in males in the sucrose and fructose groups (Figure 2D), which indicates that increased rectal glucose content caused by protein supplementation may not be the main factor affecting sex pheromones synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the glucose content data showing inconsistent effects across sugar types.

claim: YH feeding significantly increased threonine and glycine contents in males in all sugar groups.
source: On the other hand, YH feeding significantly increased threonine and glycine contents in males in all sugar groups (Figure 2E and F), which indicates that the decreased precursor amino acid contents may be the main factor affecting sex pheromone producing in rectum of YH-deprived males.
evidence: Supported by amino acid content measurements presented in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The decreased precursor amino acid contents may be the main factor affecting sex pheromone producing in rectum of YH-deprived males.
source: On the other hand, YH feeding significantly increased threonine and glycine contents in males in all sugar groups (Figure 2E and F), which indicates that the decreased precursor amino acid contents may be the main factor affecting sex pheromone producing in rectum of YH-deprived males.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the amino acid content data showing consistent effects across all sugar types.

claim: YH-deprived males were significantly different from YH-fed males based on gene expression profiles.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) using the expression profiles of the identified genes indicated that YH-deprived males were significantly different from the YH-fed ones (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: YH-fed males had higher similarity in gene expression profiles than YH-deprived individuals.
source: Pearson correlation coefficients, which were generated by the expression profiles, between samples also indicated that YH-fed males had higher similarity than YH-deprived individuals (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Pairwise differential expression analysis identified 770, 914, and 746 DE genes in the sucrose, glucose, and fructose groups, respectively.
source: Pairwise differential expression (DE) analysis identified 770, 914, and 746 DE genes in the sucrose, glucose, and fructose groups, respectively (Supplementary file 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis results presented in Supplementary file 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The glycine and threonine pathway was significantly enriched in the sucrose, glucose, and fructose groups.
source: The glycine and threonine pathway was significantly enriched in the sucrose, glucose, and fructose groups, with the sarcosine dehydrogenase gene (Sardh) and alanine-glyoxylate transaminase (AGXT2) being the significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in all groups, and the expression of Sardh was significantly induced in YH-fed males (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis presented in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Sardh and AGXT2 were the significantly differentially expressed genes in all groups.
source: The glycine and threonine pathway was significantly enriched in the sucrose, glucose, and fructose groups, with the sarcosine dehydrogenase gene (Sardh) and alanine-glyoxylate transaminase (AGXT2) being the significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in all groups, and the expression of Sardh was significantly induced in YH-fed males (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis presented in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 5.

claim: The expression of Sardh was significantly induced in YH-fed males.
source: The glycine and threonine pathway was significantly enriched in the sucrose, glucose, and fructose groups, with the sarcosine dehydrogenase gene (Sardh) and alanine-glyoxylate transaminase (AGXT2) being the significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in all groups, and the expression of Sardh was significantly induced in YH-fed males (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sardh expression was significantly enhanced by YH feeding, yet unaffected by sugar identity.
source: Quantitative PCR (qPCR) also confirmed that Sardh expression was significantly enhanced by YH feeding, yet unaffected by sugar identity (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: In the glycine and threonine metabolism pathway in insects, Sardh is responsible for converting sarcosine into glycine.
source: In the glycine and threonine metabolism pathway in insects, Sardh and L-threonine aldolase (ltaE) are responsible for converting sarcosine into glycine (Frisell and Mackenzie, 1962) and threonine (Liu et al., 1998), respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on enzyme function and illustrated in Figure 3E.

claim: In the glycine and threonine metabolism pathway in insects, ltaE is responsible for converting glycine into threonine.
source: In the glycine and threonine metabolism pathway in insects, Sardh and L-threonine aldolase (ltaE) are responsible for converting sarcosine into glycine (Frisell and Mackenzie, 1962) and threonine (Liu et al., 1998), respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on enzyme function and illustrated in Figure 3E.

claim: Sardh might be involved in sex pheromone biosynthesis by controlling glycine and threonine synthesis.
source: Together, the results suggest that Sardh might be involved in sex pheromone biosynthesis by controlling glycine and threonine synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transcriptome and amino acid content data.

claim: In normally reared male B. dorsalis, sex pheromones can only be produced 9 d after emergence.
source: In normally reared (sucrose and protein were both provided) male B. dorsalis, sex pheromones can only be produced 9 d after emergence (Ren et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on pheromone production timing.

claim: The glycine content was significantly higher in older males (6 d, 9 d, and 12 d).
source: Consistent with the idea that the glycine and threonine metabolism pathway was involved in sex pheromone biosynthesis, we found that the glycine content was significantly higher in older males (6 d, 9 d, and 12 d) (although there was no difference in the threonine content; Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by amino acid content measurements presented in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no difference in threonine content across different developmental stages.
source: Consistent with the idea that the glycine and threonine metabolism pathway was involved in sex pheromone biosynthesis, we found that the glycine content was significantly higher in older males (6 d, 9 d, and 12 d) (although there was no difference in the threonine content; Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by amino acid content measurements presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Older males had higher similarity for gene expression profiles.
source: RNA-seq data indicated that the older males had higher similarity for gene expression profiles (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by PCA and correlation analysis presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A larger number of DE genes occurred in males with greater age differences.
source: DEG analysis also indicated that a larger number of DE genes occurred in males with greater age differences (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 7.

claim: More DE genes were enriched in the glycine and threonine pathway between males with greater age differences.
source: KEGG analysis indicated that more DE genes were enriched in the glycine and threonine pathway between males with greater age differences (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis presented in Supplementary file 8.

claim: Sardh in the glycine and threonine pathway was significantly highly expressed in the rectum of older males.
source: Consistently, Sardh in the glycine and threonine pathway was significantly highly expressed in the rectum of older males (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data presented in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The high expression of Sardh in the rectum suggests that Sardh plays a role in converting YH into glycine and threonine to produce sex pheromones.
source: The high expression of Sardh in the rectum suggests that Sardh plays a role in converting YH into glycine and threonine to produce sex pheromones.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the expression data and amino acid content measurements.

claim: Sardh was highly expressed in the rectum compared to head and thorax of mature males.
source: The qPCR results showed that Sardh was indeed highly expressed in the rectum (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Sardh knockdown males showed significantly decreased rectal threonine and glycine contents.
source: Similar to YH-deprived males, Sardh knockdown males showed significantly decreased rectal threonine and glycine contents (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by amino acid content measurements in RNAi knockdown experiments presented in Figure 5B and C.

claim: TMP content in the rectum decreased significantly in Sardh knockdown males.
source: Sex pheromone quantification results indicated that TMP content in the rectum decreased significantly in Sardh knockdown males (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by sex pheromone quantification data in RNAi knockdown experiments presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Sardh knockdown males showed significantly decreased mating competition ability.
source: and that Sardh knockdown males showed significantly decreased mating competition ability (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by mating competition assay data in RNAi knockdown experiments presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Sardh plays role in converting the rectal threonine and glycine.
source: These results show that Sardh plays role in converting the rectal threonine and glycine.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNAi knockdown experiments showing decreased amino acid levels.

claim: Sardh, which can be induced by protein feeding and plays a role in synthesizing glycine and threonine, is necessary to regulate sex pheromone biosynthesis in male B. dorsalis.
source: Together, the findings provide a functional demonstration that Sardh, which can be induced by protein feeding and plays a role in synthesizing glycine and threonine, is necessary to regulate sex pheromone biosynthesis in male B. dorsalis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined transcriptome, amino acid content, and RNAi knockdown data.

claim: Pyrazines are widely used as pheromones in insects.
source: A large number of studies have indicated that pyrazines are widely used as pheromones in insects (Bohman et al., 2016; Calcagnile et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on insect pheromones.

claim: How pyrazines are synthesized in insects has not yet been revealed prior to this study.
source: However, how pyrazines are synthesized in these insects has not yet been revealed.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Protein fed by insects contributes to provide precursor substances for pyrazines synthesis.
source: With a series of chemical analysis and molecular biology experiments, we discovered that protein fed by insects contributes to provide precursor substances for pyrazines synthesis.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data from this study showing protein's role in providing amino acid precursors.

claim: The Sardh in the glycine and threonine pathway can convert protein into pyrazine precursor substances-threonine and glycine.
source: Specifically, we confirmed that the Sardh in the glycine and threonine pathway can convert protein into pyrazine precursor substances-threonine and glycine.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data showing increased amino acids with Sardh expression and decreased amino acids with Sardh knockdown.

claim: The glycine and threonine pathway is conserved in insects.
source: Given that the glycine and threonine pathway is conserved in insects (Crawford et al., 2010; Nallu et al., 2018; Sonn et al., 2018), our findings may be relevant for all insects that use protein to synthesize pyrazines.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on insect metabolic pathways.

claim: The findings may be relevant for all insects that use protein to synthesize pyrazines.
source: Given that the glycine and threonine pathway is conserved in insects (Crawford et al., 2010; Nallu et al., 2018; Sonn et al., 2018), our findings may be relevant for all insects that use protein to synthesize pyrazines.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader applicability of the findings based on pathway conservation.

claim: Previous studies suggest that the influence of protein feeding on the mating success of Tephritidae is caused by affecting the development of testes and accessory glands.
source: Previous studies suggest that the influence of protein feeding on the mating success of Tephritidae is caused by affecting the development of testes and accessory glands (Weldon and Taylor, 2011; Taylor et al., 2013; Reyes-Hernández et al., 2019) and increased levels of courtship activity (Pereira et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on tephritid reproductive biology.

claim: Previous studies suggest that the influence of protein feeding on the mating success of Tephritidae is caused by increased levels of courtship activity.
source: Previous studies suggest that the influence of protein feeding on the mating success of Tephritidae is caused by affecting the development of testes and accessory glands (Weldon and Taylor, 2011; Taylor et al., 2013; Reyes-Hernández et al., 2019) and increased levels of courtship activity (Pereira et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on tephritid behavior.

claim: Researchers have speculated that there is a positive correlation between protein feeding and sex pheromones.
source: Although researchers have speculated that there is a positive correlation between protein feeding and sex pheromones (Yuval et al., 2007), this relationship has been hard to pin down.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research that speculated about this relationship.

claim: The relationship between protein feeding and sex pheromones has been hard to pin down prior to this study.
source: Although researchers have speculated that there is a positive correlation between protein feeding and sex pheromones (Yuval et al., 2007), this relationship has been hard to pin down.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Certain plant chemicals, such as methyl eugenol, gingerone, and raspberry ketone, strongly attract tephritidae males of some species.
source: Certain plant chemicals, such as methyl eugenol, gingerone, and raspberry ketone, which strongly attract tephritidae males of some species, are thought to be the precursors of sex pheromones (Tan and Nishida, 2012; Kumaran et al., 2014a, Kumaran et al., 2014b, Segura et al., 2018), and a variety of chemicals have been identified and proposed as sex pheromone components in fruit flies (Chuman et al., 1987; Baker and Heath, 1993; Wicker-Thomas, 2007; Robacker et al., 2009; Hiap et al., 2019; Levi-Zada et al., 2020; Ono et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on tephritid chemical ecology.

claim: Certain plant chemicals are thought to be the precursors of sex pheromones in tephritidae.
